"title": "From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving",
"authors": "Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu",
"field_subfield": "Robotics / Autonomous Driving",
"type_of_paper": "Preprint",
"executive_summary": "Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically customizes autonomous-driving policies to match natural-language user commands, without relying on prior driving data. The authors argue that current AVs suffer from a uniform driving style, which contributes to rear-end crashes and a poor user experience, and that existing methods either depend on expert-designed styles or on data-driven Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), both of which struggle with data scarcity, metric misalignment, and the generalization problem. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function that bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, using large language models (LLMs) and a Driving Style Database to retrieve, adapt, and generalize styles, with a Statistical Evaluation module to ensure alignment with user preferences. The system is grounded in a Markov Decision Process formulation and trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Experiments used the HighD dataset (4K drone camera) with a 15% reserved test set, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 at temperature 0.3, k=3, and n=2. Words2Wheels was benchmarked against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) using 10 licensed volunteers across 1,000 tested events. In 72% of events, participants judged Words2Wheels as a better match than IDM, versus 9.2% for IDM, with 18.8% ties. The authors also report generation capability, generalization capability, human-in-the-loop comparisons, generalization capability, and fuzzy memory functionality. The paper claims Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies aligned with natural-language commands, and highlights future work including expanding to complex scenarios, refining the Statistical Evaluation module, and incorporating a Feedback and Reflection module. Code and demo are available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/.",

Existing methods either depend on predefined styles requiring expert input or use data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), which face challenges in obtaining specific driving data, aligning metrics with user preferences, and generalizing to new commands. summary.title: From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving
summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu
summary.executive_summary: Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically customizes autonomous-driving policies to match natural-language user commands without relying on prior driving data. The authors argue that current AVs suffer from a uniform driving style, which is a safety and experience problem, and that existing methods either depend on predefined styles requiring expert input or use data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that struggle with data availability, metric alignment, and generalization. The core innovation is a Style-Customized Reward Function that bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, enabled by large language models (LLMs) and a Driving Style Database. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences by comparing generated policies against natural driving behavior on a reserved test set. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to select relevant style rewards, generates new reward functions when no match exists, and trains new policies via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), replacing existing policies when the new ones perform better. Experiments used the HighD dataset with a car-following scenario, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base model, and temperature 0.3. In human-in-the-loop comparisons against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM), Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of events, with 18.8% ties and only 9.2% preference for IDM. The framework demonstrates strong accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, and includes a fuzzy memory function for recalling similar commands. Code and demo are available online. The paper positions itself as the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies aligned with natural language commands, and outlines future work including expanding to more complex scenarios and adding a Feedback and Reflection module.

claims.description: Words2Wheels automatically customizes driving policies to align with natural language user commands without relying on prior driving data.
Words2Wheels outperforms existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically customizes autonomous-driving policies to match natural-language user commands without relying on prior driving data. The authors argue that current AVs suffer from a uniform driving style, which is a safety and experience problem, and that existing methods either depend on predefined styles requiring expert input or use data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that struggle with data availability, metric alignment, and generalization. The core innovation is a Style-Customized Reward Function that bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, enabled by large language models (LLMs) and a Driving Style Database. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences by comparing generated policies against natural driving behavior on a reserved test set. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to select relevant style rewards, generates new reward functions when no match exists, and trains new policies via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), replacing existing policies when the new ones perform better. Experiments used the HighD dataset with a car-following scenario, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base model, and temperature 0.3. In human-in-the-loop comparisons against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM), Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of events, with 18.8% ties and only 9.2% preference for IDM. The framework demonstrates strong accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, and includes a fuzzy memory function for recalling similar commands. Code and demo are available online. The paper positions itself as the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies aligned with natural language commands, and outlines future work including expanding to more complex scenarios and adding a Feedback and Reflection module.

Research Context
Autonomous driving has advanced with foundation models improving interactivity and user experience. A key criticism is the uniform driving style of current autonomous vehicles. 52.46% of AVs involved in crashes were rear-ended, 1.6 times the rate of conventional vehicles. Early approaches relied heavily on classification or calibration of predefined styles or driving patterns. Data-driven approaches use clustering and IRL to derive driving policies from natural driving behavior data. These methods face challenges in data availability, metric alignment, and generalization. Foundation models process user instructions but fall short at the style level. These approaches raise concerns about reliability and efficiency.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether Words2Wheels can automatically customize driving policies to align with natural language user commands. The hypothesis is that a Style-Customized Reward Function can bridge user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy without prior driving data. The framework leverages LLMs and RAG to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences. Words2Wheels is hypothesized to outperform existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability. The system can generalize to new commands without user behavior data via zero-shot generation. New policies that outperform existing ones can replace them, expanding the style range.

Methodological Details
The study focused on the car-following scenario as the experimental focus. The experiment utilized the HighD dataset collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone. Data extraction and kinematic model were based on FollowNet. 15% of the data was reserved as a test set to ensure objectivity. User commands were categorized into three levels based on directness. Level I commands are direct, Level II are indirect with strong hints, and Level III are indirect with mild hints. The base model was GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature set to 0.3. k was set to 3 in selecting relevant styles and n was set to 2 in Statistical Evaluation. The Driving Style Database was populated with 8 initial styles. Some styles were data-driven reward functions derived using clustering plus IRL. Others were human-designed reward functions based on prior methodologies. Style Policies are stored as pre-trained neural networks. Analytical data can be saved in JSON format. Metrics include speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing, and time headway. The Statistical Evaluation module uses a Chain-of-Thought approach. Human participants were recruited with valid driving licenses. Each participant was presented with 5 user commands and 20 events per command. This resulted in a total of 1,000 tested events. The fuzzy memory function was tested with 3 experimental sets. Each set tested 5 similar inputs to see if the system could recall the corresponding memory.

Procedures And Architectures
The process starts by applying RAG principles where the LLM selects the top k relevant style rewards. This step can be parallelized for efficiency. If a selected Style Reward has matched a semantically similar command, the Style Policy is used directly. If no match is found, the LLM generates m new reward functions based on the most relevant Style Reward. The LLM's generation may involve logic modifications or restructuring. The initially selected Style Reward provides a temporary solution since its policy is already trained. Newly generated reward functions produce new Style Policies via RL, where trainings can be parallelized. Words2Wheels uses Proximal Policy Optimization for training. RL training was run 5 times using different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. Words2Wheels determines if the new policies outperform the temporary one. The data was normalized using the 10th and 90th percentiles of the natural driving behavior. The Statistical Evaluation module prompts the LLM to answer in JSON format. The visualization tool displays clips of car-following behavior from two different models. The models are anonymized as A and B to eliminate bias. Future work will incorporate a Feedback and Reflection module.

Key Results
The aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration. The conservative style maintained a larger gap and relative speed. The aggressive style had a larger time headway. The normal style showed higher jerk. Words2Wheels demonstrated a strong ability to adapt to different driving styles. When the input was 'I'm going to be late for the train,' the generated style exhibited higher speed, acceleration, and jerk. When the input was 'Safety first. I have plenty of time,' the generated style showed greater spacing, time headway, and relative speed. Words2Wheels can generate driving styles that align with user commands rather than simply selecting from existing styles. In 72% of events, participants judged Words2Wheels to be a better match to the user command than IDM. In 18.8% of events, both models were considered equally effective. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events. For Level I commands, retrieval was 100% and analysis was 100%. For Level III commands, retrieval was 90% and generation was 85%. Overall, Words2Wheels performed well in terms of analysis, decision-making, and generation. The system's handling of Level I commands was slightly more accurate than for Level II and III commands. With the exception of one case involving 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased,' all other test cases were successfully recalled. The system demonstrated a strong ability to recognize and match fuzzy inputs to existing memories.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Words2Wheels bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy via a Style-Customized Reward Function. The reward function guides the driving policy to optimize long-term rewards and serves as a policy index. Style Rewards are less complex than user commands or traffic scenarios, enabling efficient retrieval of Style Policy. The framework generalizes to new commands and styles without user behavior data via zero-shot generation. The Driving Style Database enables efficient retrieval and continuous enrichment of driving styles. The Statistical Evaluation module automatically and accurately measures alignment between driving policies and user commands. Words2Wheels is the first framework that automatically customizes style-aware driving policies to align with natural language user commands. The fuzzy memory function enhances the adaptability of the driving models. The system reduces reliance on RL as the database expands. The framework is extensible, allowing for features like fuzzy memory via LLMs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style had a larger time headway, which may contradict expectations. The normal style showed higher jerk, possibly because the LLM did not prioritize these metrics. In a few isolated cases, the LLM's interpretation and processing were off. In Case 19, the LLM misinterpreted the user command 'You are allowing a large gap with the vehicle in front.' In Case 26, the LLM intentionally selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk value as a counterexample. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. The study focused only on the car-following scenario. The Statistical Evaluation module may require refinement for finer tuning. The base model GPT-4o-2024-08-06 may limit generalizability. The temperature was set to 0.3 for more deterministic text generation. The number of initial styles was limited to 4 for better demonstration in some experiments. The fuzzy memory function had one failure case involving 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased.' The study is a preprint version. The paper is a preprint, which may limit its reliability.

Claims
Words2Wheels automatically customizes driving policies to align with natural language user commands without relying on prior driving data. The framework automatically generates customized driving policies based on natural language user commands. The system uses a Style-Customized Reward Function to generate a Style-Customized Driving Policy. The framework leverages LLMs and RAG to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles. The system can generalize to new commands without user behavior data. In a few isolated cases, the LLM's interpretation and processing were off. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. Words2Wheels offers a novel solution for customized AV driving behavior. The framework improves user experience in autonomous vehicles through style customization. The fuzzy memory function enhances the adaptability of the driving models.
Words2Wheels outperforms existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability. In 72% of events, participants judged Words2Wheels to be a better match to the user command than IDM. Words2Wheels can generate driving styles that align with user commands rather than simply selecting from existing styles. Words2Wheels demonstrated a strong ability to adapt to different driving styles. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events, but 18.8% were ties. The aggressive style had a larger time headway, which may not align with expectations. The framework reduces reliance on RL as the database expands. The system is extensible, allowing for features like fuzzy memory via LLMs.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo are available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/. Experimental records are available at https://bit.ly/4giYhB7. The HighD dataset was used for the experiments.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
RL training was run 5 times using different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. Each command was run 5 times and the outcomes were averaged. Results from 5 repeated runs were averaged in the generation capability experiment. The data was normalized using the 10th and 90th percentiles of the natural driving behavior. The models were anonymized as A and B to eliminate bias.

Ethical Considerations
The models were anonymized as A and B to eliminate bias. We recruited 10 volunteers with valid driving license. The study is a preprint version.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the workflow of Words2Wheels, where a natural language command is matched with a style from the database. Fig. 2 shows the Driving Style Database, which stores Style Rewards, Style Policies, and their statistics. Fig. 3 shows an example of automated Style Policy generation. Fig. 4 shows a simplified example of the Statistical Evaluation module. Fig. 5 shows the comparison of customized policies over style-aware metrics. Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Words2Wheels framework that automatically customizes driving policies to align with natural language user commands. 2. The strongest evidence is the 72% preference rate in human-in-the-loop comparisons against IDM. 3. The future path is expanding the framework to more complex driving scenarios and adding a Feedback and Reflection module.
